2026-08-05.headline: Note: 5 Aug figures are intraday prints; the last confirmed close is Tuesday 4 Aug. The integrity check clears — the 4 Aug row has refreshed with true closes. Score HOLDS at 27/30. No channel moved. Two things happened, and they run in opposite directions. First, the market took the war premium out with both hands. Brent closed $77.93 on Tuesday, $3.16 below Monday and $10.00 below Friday’s close — the largest two-session fall since 6 May and the lowest close since 10 July, and it did so alongside a 6.3 bp fall in the 10Y close and 5.3 bp in the 30Y. That drags Stage-4 Threshold B out of satisfaction for the first time since 28 July: the 30Y closed 5.1743% against its 5.20% leg and the 10Y 4.6126% against its 4.65% leg, ending a four-close run that included two war records. It also puts the oil channel’s downgrade anchor within $5.45 — the narrowest that gap has been since 10 July. Second, and this is why nothing moved, the diplomacy this monitor could not source yesterday has acquired a real and differently-constituted form. Iran now publicly confirms a negotiation — but with Oman, not with Washington. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Tuesday that Tehran is in bilateral talks with Muscat on safe inbound and outbound shipping lanes; Secretary of State Rubio said there had been ‘progress made in those talks, but not finality yet’; and Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC ‘there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait.’ Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman said in the same 24 hours that no direct US–Iran talks are scheduled. This is the first negotiating track of the war that both sides confirm, and it is the first credible route to a maritime downgrade. It is also not a stand-down: a Liberian-flagged bulk carrier, the Minoan Pioneer, was struck about 20 nm north-east of Khasab on Tuesday with one crew member missing, and the deal on the table is conditional on Washington lifting a blockade no US official has publicly committed to lifting. Five of six channels remain maxed. Only oil, at 2/5, can raise this number — and for the first time it is closer to falling than to rising. Sequencing 26 → 27 → 27.

THE IRAN–OMAN CORRIDOR TALKS ADVANCE — AND FOR THE FIRST TIME IN THIS WAR BOTH SIDES CONFIRM A NEGOTIATION

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on 4 Aug that Tehran is negotiating bilaterally with Oman on establishing safe inbound and outbound shipping lanes, respecting Iranian sovereignty and both states’ security needs, and that ‘the final results of these negotiations will be announced once concluded’. AP and CBS News report the architecture as inbound Gulf traffic via an Iranian-controlled route and outbound via an Omani-controlled route, with security and environmental fees split, broad outlines agreed and the implementation timeline unresolved — and conditional on Washington lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Secretary of State Rubio said ‘there’s been progress made in those talks, but not finality yet’. Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC ‘there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait’ and, on tolls, ‘I think it would be freedom of movement.’ No agreement has been signed.
AP / CBS News / ABC News / Al Jazeera / CNBC
A bulk carrier was struck in the strait in the same 24 hours

The Liberian-flagged, Greek-owned bulk carrier Minoan Pioneer was struck by an unidentified projectile about 20 nm north-east of Khasab, Oman on 4 Aug, suffering a complete electrical blackout and a fire in the accommodation block, with one crew member missing; the cause is unattributed. Separately the Indian vessel MSV Faize Noore Oliya capsized and sank after a projectile strike near Yemen with all 14 crew rescued, and the Houthis claimed a drone strike on Najran airport in Saudi Arabia, a claim not independently confirmed. Aramco’s chief executive said recent Houthi attacks had no material impact on production capability. No Tier 1 outlet reported a new US or Israeli strike on Iran on 4 or 5 Aug; CENTCOM has issued no strike release since 29 Jul.
CBS News / AP / Splash247 / Riviera Maritime / CENTCOM
Washington talks the deal up; Qatar and Iran both say there is no US–Iran channel

President Trump said on 4 Aug ‘we are, in fact, talking’, and attributed his cancellation of the strike package to pressure from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said the same day that no direct US–Iran talks are currently scheduled, and that Qatar, Oman and Pakistan are working jointly to ‘create appropriate conditions’. Pezeshkian said Iran will defend its borders but is ‘not seeking to expand the war’. Reuters and CBS News reported that the US has expended ‘virtually all’ of its ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, with Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell disputing the characterisation.
AP / ABC News / CBS News / Reuters / Al Jazeera
Two dated tests land today; the physical supply picture is unchanged

The Treasury quarterly refunding statement is due at 8:30am ET on Wednesday 5 Aug and the EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report at 10:30am ET — both AFTER this Singapore-morning snapshot, and neither is in this edition. Monday’s borrowing estimate of $739bn for July–September stands, $68bn above the 4 May projection. On the physical side nothing changed: OPEC+ added 188k b/d for September against effective spare capacity the IEA put at about 0.17 mb/d in July; Aramco’s 400k b/d Jizan complex is targeted to restart about 15 Aug on a Reuters report citing IIR; Abqaiq and Damietta remain unreported since late July. US data on 4 Aug: JOLTS job openings 7.4 million and little changed, and the June goods and services trade deficit narrowing to $73.3bn from a revised $77.6bn.

analysis.intro: The shock holds at 27/30 and no channel moved, but the composition of the risk changed more in this session than in the last three combined. The market de-risked hard: Brent’s 4 August close of $77.93 is $10.00 below Friday’s, the largest two-session fall since 6 May, and the entire Treasury curve closed 5.8 to 7.3 bp below the Singapore-morning snapshot. That has a mechanical consequence — Stage-4 Threshold B, satisfied on four consecutive closes including two war records, is no longer satisfied — and a directional one: the oil channel’s downgrade anchor is now $5.45 away, closer than at any point since 10 July. The news moved the other way in form but the same way in substance. The negotiation this monitor could not source on Monday exists after all, but it is an Iran–Oman corridor negotiation that Tehran confirms and a US–Iran negotiation that Qatar and Tehran both deny. That is a materially better-evidenced diplomatic track than the one revoked yesterday, and it is the first credible route to a MARITIME downgrade rather than an escalation one. It is not a stand-down: a bulk carrier was struck off Khasab in the same 24 hours with a crew member missing, and the deal is conditional on Washington lifting a blockade it has not offered to lift.

bondYield.title: (i) Treasury — held at 5 (max), and Stage-4 Threshold B has LAPSED.
bondYield.text: This is the move of the edition even though no score changed. The 30Y closed 5.1743% on 4 August and the 10Y 4.6126%, so both legs of Threshold B failed on the same close — the first failure since 28 July and the end of a four-close run that included the 5.2724% and 4.7347% war records of 31 July. This morning’s 5.1806% and 4.6228% leave the threshold unsatisfied on a second session, by 1.94 bp and 2.72 bp. The lapse should be read precisely: it does not repair the long end, which still sits 57.0 bp above its pre-war anchor and 12.43 bp above the 13 May auction stop, and it does not move the channel, which is at its maximum and governed by a downgrade requiring a 30Y close under 5.00% with MOVE under 75. Those legs still fail by 17.43 bp and 2.56 pts. But both have narrowed materially: on Monday they failed by 22.74 bp and 5.48 pts. MOVE closed 77.56, down 2.92 on the session and 5.46 from Friday’s spike, its lowest since 30 July. What makes this the wrong session to conclude anything is the calendar: the quarterly refunding statement lands at 8:30am ET today, hours after this snapshot, against Monday’s $739bn borrowing estimate and 6 May guidance holding coupon sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn ‘for at least the next several quarters’. A long end whose 30Y closed 5.3 bp lower into that statement has pre-positioned for the guidance to survive.

bondYield.title: (ii) Oil — held at 2, and for the first time in the war it is closer to a downgrade than an upgrade.
bondYield.text: The last confirmed close is $77.93 (4 August), $17.07 below the $95 upgrade trigger and $5.45 above the $72.48 downgrade anchor — the narrowest that gap has been since 10 July, and narrower than the $8.61 of Monday. Brent has fallen $10.00 in two sessions from the 31 July close, the largest two-session decline since 6 May, and prints $77.76 this morning in a 71-cent range entirely below Tuesday’s close. WTI’s $74.40 close is likewise the lowest since 10 July. The downgrade requires both legs: a mediated pause AND a close at or below $72.48. The price leg is now within reach on any two sessions like the last two. The pause leg is NOT satisfied and the monitor is explicit about why: a corridor negotiation is not a pause, and a bulk carrier was struck in the strait on the same day the negotiation was confirmed. The physical case for a higher number is also unchanged — effective OPEC+ spare capacity was roughly 0.17 mb/d on the IEA’s July estimate so September’s 188k b/d is a quota rather than a cargo, Jizan’s 400k b/d is out to about 15 August, Abqaiq and Damietta are unreported, and the strait is shut on day 157 — which is precisely the point. The market has repriced the probability of a settlement, not the physical balance. If the corridor deal is signed, this channel can fall to 1 and take the score with it; if it is not, $77.93 with 0.17 mb/d of spare capacity is a fragile price.

bondYield.title: (iii) Escalation risk — held at 5 (max). The downgrade candidate is re-opened, on a different and better-sourced track, and still not taken.
bondYield.text: Yesterday this monitor revoked a downgrade candidate because the negotiation it rested on could not be sourced. Today a negotiation can be sourced, and it is not the same one. Baghaei confirmed on the record that Iran is in bilateral talks with Oman on shipping lanes; Rubio confirmed US involvement in that channel and said there had been progress but ‘not finality yet’; Bessent said a deal to open the strait might come ‘today or tomorrow’. That is the first time in this war that Tehran and Washington have described the same negotiation as existing. It is also, on its face, less than the channel needs. Qatar’s spokesman said no direct US–Iran talks are scheduled; the President’s ‘we are, in fact, talking’ is still contradicted by the mediator and by Tehran; the deal is conditional on lifting a blockade Washington has not offered to lift; and the Minoan Pioneer was struck off Khasab on 4 August with a crew member missing. A stand-down cannot be found in a window that contains a vessel casualty. The correct read is that the downgrade path has moved from ‘unsourceable’ to ‘real but unconsummated’ in one session, and that the channel most likely to move first is maritime, not escalation.

bondYield.title: (iv) US inflation impulse — held at 5 (max), and the forward is the last thing standing.
bondYield.text: 5Y5Y forward inflation closed 2.3180% on 4 August, a sixth consecutive close above the 2.30% trigger and a third consecutive decline from the 2.3597% war record. It has given back 4.17 bp in total. Set that against what everything else did in the same window: Brent gave back $10.00, and the 10Y breakeven closed 2.2278% — its first close below the 2.2569% pre-war anchor since 28 July, having given back 5.68 bp from its 31 July high. Spot inflation compensation has fully round-tripped the war premium it built in July; the forward has given back a quarter of it. That divergence is the whole argument for this channel sitting at 5. A market that thought this was an energy shock would have taken the forward down with the crude. The downgrade — 5Y5Y sustained at or below the 2.142% anchor — is 17.6 bp away and not in play, though it is 2.0 bp closer than on Monday. At 5/5 the channel can only subtract, and today it did not.

bondYield.title: (v) Political stress — held at 5 (max), the upgrade reinforced and the corroboration diverging.
bondYield.text: AUTMUSAG has backfilled 3 August at $4.76, a third consecutive confirmed close above the $4.75 trigger after 30 and 31 July. The 4→5 upgrade fired last edition is therefore better evidenced than when it fired, not worse. The series is blank for 4 and 5 August — three of the last five sessions dark — and is flagged rather than carried. The more interesting development is corroborative: the DOE weekly series flagged as missing last edition has backfilled at $4.079 for the week to 3 August, down 1.7 cents from $4.096, matching EIA’s own release to the tenth of a cent, and AAA’s separately published regular-grade national average printed $4.089 on 4 August against $4.099 a week earlier. The corroborating retail series are easing while the scored series holds at its highs — the first such divergence since June. Two things follow. First, the upgrade stands on three confirmed closes and hysteresis requires a sustained reversal past a wider threshold to undo it, so an easing corroborator does not reverse it. Second, the next AUTMUSAG print is now a genuine test rather than a formality. What is not easing is diesel: EIA had on-highway diesel at $5.348 for the week to 3 August, and refining rather than crude remains the binding constraint on the pump — which is why Brent at $77.93 does not disarm this channel.

bondYield.title: (vi) Maritime denial — held at 5 (max), and this is now the channel most likely to move next.
bondYield.text: The strait is closed on day 157 and the traffic data is not close to the downgrade condition on any tracker: Kpler has 106 all-crossings in the week to 2 August against 98 the week before with about 41% route-undetermined; Windward logged 12 identified transits in the 24 hours to 2 August with half of them dark; TankerMap counted 2 tanker transits on 3 August and none at all on 4 August; CBS News reports 45 commercial vessels redirected since the blockade was reinstated. Against a pre-war baseline that different sources put anywhere between 73 and 130 crossings a day, none of these readings is within reach of traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. What has changed is the instrument. A signed Iran–Oman corridor agreement — inbound via an Iranian-controlled route, outbound via an Omani-controlled route, fees split — is exactly the event that starts that ten-session clock, and two cabinet-level US officials said on 4 August that it may be days or hours away. It is still unsigned, its implementation timeline is unresolved, and it is conditional on the US lifting its port blockade. The channel does not move on an announcement; it moves on ten sessions of verified traffic.

analysis.stage4Note: Stage 4 is a credit/auction event. Threshold B has LAPSED after four consecutive satisfied closes, and the refunding statement that quantifies the supply test lands hours after this snapshot.

stage4.title: Threshold A · 13 May 30Y auction, cleared 5.050% — the test is dated for today.
stage4.text: Historical benchmark; the 9 July re-opening cleared 5.06% with a 0.3 bp stop-through. The 4 August close of 5.1743% is 12.43 bp above the May stop, down from 17.74 bp on Monday and 22.24 bp at Friday’s war-widest. Treasury said on Monday it expects to borrow $739bn of net marketable debt in July–September against the $671bn projected on 4 May, and $628bn in October–December, on assumed cash balances of $950bn at end-September and $850bn at end-December. The quarterly refunding statement follows at 8:30am ET today, Wednesday 5 August — after this snapshot and not in this edition — against 6 May guidance holding coupon sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn ‘for at least the next several quarters’. The 30Y leg auctions in the week of 10 August. The specific sequence that would make Threshold A live rather than historical is unchanged: a coupon-size increase today, followed by a weak 30Y leg next week, into a long end still 57 bp above its pre-war anchor. Tuesday’s 5.8 bp rally is the market betting that does not happen.

stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — NO LONGER SATISFIED.
stage4.text: The run was 29 July 5.2007% / 4.6773%, 30 July 5.2135% / 4.6733%, 31 July 5.2724% / 4.7347% (both war records) and 3 August 5.2274% / 4.6755%. On 4 August both legs failed together for the first time since 28 July: 5.1743% is 2.57 bp below its leg and 4.6126% is 3.74 bp below its own. This morning’s 5.1806% and 4.6228% keep it unsatisfied on a second session. Three qualifications belong with this. First, a persistence threshold that lapses after four closes has done its job — it warned, and the warning has partially unwound; it has not been falsified. Second, the unwind was a risk-premium unwind across every asset in the same session, not a repair of the fiscal arithmetic that armed the threshold: Treasury still needs $68bn more this quarter than it said in May. Third, the threshold can re-arm on a single bad auction, and the auction is next week. The correct reading is that the long end has bought itself a fortnight, not that the test has passed.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130. Far off, and easing for a second session.
stage4.text: The index closed 77.56 on 4 August, down 2.92 and 5.46 below Friday’s 83.02, its lowest since 30 July. That leaves 52.44 pts to the threshold and keeps it well under the 115.02 war high of 26 March, so C is not close. The observation that matters is the other one: at 77.56 the index is only 2.56 pts above the 75 line that forms the second leg of the Treasury downgrade, the narrowest since 29 July. For the first time in the war the two Treasury downgrade legs are simultaneously within a fortnight’s ordinary range of each other — but they must be satisfied together, and the 30Y is still 17.43 bp above its own. There is no 5 August print and the number is flagged rather than carried as fresh.

analysis.crossAsset: The cross-asset signature this session is a single, coherent, one-directional de-risking — and it is the exact mirror of last Friday. Every field in the extract came in below the value published for it yesterday morning except one: Brent $77.93 against $81.92, WTI $74.40 against $78.66, TTF €55.921 against €58.260, the 30Y 5.1743% against 5.2327%, the 10Y 4.6126% against 4.6858%, the 2Y 4.1917% against 4.2519%, 5Y5Y 2.3180% against 2.3376%, MOVE 77.56 against a carried 80.48, DXY 99.858 against 100.011. The single exception is VIX, up 0.64 to 16.50. On 31 July every field came in ABOVE the snapshot and Brent was $1.97 higher; on 4 August every field came in below and Brent was $3.99 lower. Those are the two largest reconciliation gaps this monitor has recorded, four sessions apart, in opposite directions. What that says is not that the snapshot is unreliable in a random way — it is that the US session is now doing all the price discovery, in one direction per day, on headlines that land after Singapore closes. Underneath the move, the routing signature is intact and strengthening: Henry Hub at $2.693 is 12.1% BELOW pre-war and its 4 August close is the lowest since 29 April, while Asia LNG rose to ¥3,440 and TTF fell for a third session. US gas is not participating in this war, which is the clearest evidence available that it remains a Hormuz-routing shock rather than a global-energy shock. The reading to take is that the market has priced a strait reopening it has not yet been shown.

whatsChanged.title: 4 · What's changed since the last edition (4 Aug AM → 5 Aug AM)
items: Score holds at 27/30; no channel moved. Stage-4 Threshold B lapses. Brent falls $10.00 in two sessions. Iran confirms an Oman corridor negotiation. A bulk carrier is struck off Khasab. Source: Bloomberg unless stated.

Stage-4 Threshold B is no longer satisfied, after four consecutive closes including two war records. The 30Y closed 5.1743% and the 10Y 4.6126% on 4 August, failing both legs of the 30Y-above-5.20%-with-10Y-above-4.65% test together for the first time since 28 July. The run it ends was 29 July 5.2007% / 4.6773%, 30 July 5.2135% / 4.6733%, 31 July 5.2724% / 4.7347% and 3 August 5.2274% / 4.6755%. This morning’s 5.1806% and 4.6228% keep it unsatisfied on a second session. The Treasury channel does not move — it is at its maximum and its downgrade needs a 30Y close under 5.00% with MOVE under 75, which still fail by 17.43 bp and 2.56 pts. Source: Bloomberg.

Brent fell $10.00 in two sessions to its lowest close since 10 July, and the oil downgrade anchor is now $5.45 away. The 4 August close of $77.93 is $3.16 below Monday and $10.00 below Friday’s $87.93 — the largest two-session decline since 6 May. It is $17.07 below the $95 upgrade trigger and $5.45 above the $72.48 downgrade anchor, the narrowest that gap has been since 10 July. WTI’s $74.40 close is likewise the lowest since 10 July. The channel holds at 2 because the downgrade needs a mediated pause as well as the price, and there is no pause. Source: Bloomberg.

Iran publicly confirmed a negotiation for the first time in this war — with Oman, not with Washington. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on 4 August that Tehran is in bilateral talks with Oman on establishing safe inbound and outbound shipping lanes, respecting Iranian sovereignty and both states’ security needs, and that results would be announced only once concluded. AP and CBS News report the architecture as inbound via an Iranian-controlled route and outbound via an Omani-controlled route with security and environmental fees split, broad outlines agreed, implementation timeline unresolved, and the whole conditional on Washington lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Secretary of State Rubio said there had been ‘progress made in those talks, but not finality yet’. Source: AP / CBS News / ABC News / Al Jazeera.

Two US cabinet officials publicly forecast a strait deal within days, while Qatar said no US–Iran talks are scheduled. Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC on 4 August: ‘There is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait,’ and on tolls, ‘I think it would be freedom of movement.’ President Trump said ‘we are, in fact, talking’ and attributed his cancellation of the strike package to pressure from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said the same day that no direct US–Iran talks are currently scheduled and that Qatar, Oman and Pakistan are working jointly to create appropriate conditions. Washington is talking up a deal it is not formally party to. Source: CNBC via AP / ABC News / CBS News.

A bulk carrier was struck in the strait, with one crew member missing. The Liberian-flagged, Greek-owned Minoan Pioneer was struck by an unidentified projectile about 20 nm north-east of Khasab, Oman on 4 August, suffering a complete electrical blackout and a fire in the accommodation block; one crew member is missing and the cause is unattributed. Separately the Indian vessel MSV Faize Noore Oliya sank after a projectile strike near Yemen with all 14 crew rescued, and the Houthis claimed a drone strike on Najran airport in Saudi Arabia, which Aramco’s chief executive said had no material impact on production. This is why the escalation channel is not downgraded on a negotiation. Source: CBS News / AP / Splash247 / Riviera Maritime.

Tuesday’s reconciliation was the largest DOWNSIDE gap the monitor has recorded — the mirror of 31 July. Every field in the extract came in below the intraday value published for it yesterday except one. Brent $77.93 against $81.92 (−$3.99); WTI $74.40 vs $78.66; TTF €55.921 vs €58.260; 30Y 5.1743% vs 5.2327% (−5.84 bp); 10Y 4.6126% vs 4.6858% (−7.32 bp); 2Y 4.1917% vs 4.2519% (−6.02 bp); 5Y5Y 2.3180% vs 2.3376%; BE10 2.2278% vs 2.2603%; DXY 99.858 vs 100.011; MOVE an actual 77.56 against a carried 80.48. The exception is VIX, an actual 16.50 against a carried 15.86. Four sessions ago every field came in ABOVE the snapshot. Source: Bloomberg.

The DOE gasoline weekly backfilled and turned DOWN, while the scored series backfilled a third close above its trigger. AUTMUSAG has backfilled 3 August at $4.76 — a third consecutive confirmed close above the $4.75 political trigger, reinforcing the 4→5 upgrade fired last edition. USRFRUSA has backfilled the week to 3 August at $4.079, down 1.7 cents from $4.096, and it matches EIA’s own Gasoline and Diesel Fuel Update released 4 August to the tenth of a cent. AAA’s separately published regular-grade national average printed $4.089 on 4 August against $4.099 a week earlier. The corroborating series are easing while the scored series holds — the first divergence since June. Source: Bloomberg / EIA / AAA.

Correction: the 4 August edition mis-read a narrow snapshot range as a quiet session. The session was violent. That edition wrote that Brent’s ‘very narrow intraday range of 74 cents’ showed the market had ‘stopped trading headlines’. The full 4 August session ran a $6.13 range, from $83.35 to $77.22, the second-widest of the last fortnight after 31 July’s $6.74, and closed $3.99 below the snapshot. The snapshot range measures the Singapore morning and carries no information about the US session. That inference is withdrawn. Source: Bloomberg.

Correction: the strike-planning story was Tier 1 from the start, and the crediting in the last two editions was wrong. The 3 August edition carried US/Israeli planning against Iranian civilian energy infrastructure as a single-outlet Al Jazeera item, and the 4 August edition credited CBS News with corroborating it. Re-verification finds the story originated with Axios (Barak Ravid) on 31 July, reporting that Trump was considering strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure including power plants and bridges within days, sourced to a US official and to Trump’s own cabinet remarks; the Wall Street Journal reported the same day that an attack had been ordered for that weekend. Al Jazeera’s 1 August piece explicitly attributed the claim to ‘major US media outlets’ and was derivative. The correct status is: Tier 1 from the outset, and SHELVED on 2 August when Trump cancelled the package — not disavowed. No Tier 1 outlet has reported its revival and no US official has denied it. Source: Axios / WSJ / Al Jazeera / Washington Post / NBC News.

Correction: the Iraqi militia deadline is NOT corroborated above Tier 3, and there is one date, not two. The 4 August edition promoted this item, citing Rudaw for a 7 August deadline and Ynetnews for a 6 August Kataib Hezbollah deadline. Re-verification finds the 7 August date originated with Press TV on 29 July — Tier 3 — with regional Tier 2 pickup by Shafaq News, Rudaw and Middle East Monitor on 30 July. No Tier 1 outlet carries either date. The 6 August date could not be re-sourced. The item reverts to Tier 3 origination with Tier 2 pickup, exactly as the 3 August edition had it, and should not be used for anything market-moving. Source: Press TV (Tier 3) / Shafaq / Rudaw / MEMO.

US data on 4 August was soft-to-neutral; the two tests that matter land today, after this snapshot. JOLTS job openings for June were little changed at 7.4 million, with hires 5.3m, quits 3.2m and layoffs 1.8m all unchanged. The June goods and services trade deficit narrowed 5.6% to $73.3bn from a revised $77.6bn. ISM manufacturing for July, released 3 August, printed 55.6 with the prices index at 71.1, its 22nd consecutive monthly increase. The Treasury quarterly refunding statement is due 8:30am ET today and the EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report at 10:30am ET — the first EIA weekly since the 24 July print, which had SPR at 307.7 mb after a 3.7 mb draw. Neither is in this edition. Source: BLS / BEA / ISM / US Treasury / EIA.

scenarios.name: Return to full war
scenarios.desc: Lower, and for the first time since 30 Jul it is falling rather than rising — though still the modal path. The strike package was cancelled on 2 Aug and no Tier 1 outlet has reported its revival; CENTCOM has issued no strike release since 29 Jul, seven days; and Trump attributed the cancellation to pressure from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Reuters and CBS report the US has expended ‘virtually all’ of its ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, which the Pentagon disputes but which bears on capacity for a sustained campaign.
scenarios.path: Brent $105–140; MOVE above 90; oil to 3–4; score 28–29 (only oil can rise).

scenarios.name: Deal collapse — talks stall on terms
scenarios.desc: Higher, and now the largest non-war line. The Iran–Oman corridor track is real and confirmed by both sides, which is exactly why its failure conditions are now specific rather than hypothetical: it is conditional on Washington lifting its port blockade, which no US official has publicly committed to; Rubio says ‘not finality yet’; Baghaei says results will be announced only once concluded; and the toll question — Bessent’s ‘freedom of movement’ against Iranian fee proposals — is unresolved.
scenarios.path: Brent $88–105; oil back toward 3; Threshold B re-arms; score 28.

scenarios.name: Contained but violent — blockaded stalemate
scenarios.desc: Higher. The strait is shut on day 157 with TankerMap counting zero tanker transits on 4 Aug, a bulk carrier was struck off Khasab with a crew member missing, and the score sits at 27 regardless because five of six channels are pinned at 5. This is the path in which the market’s repricing turns out to have been premature and nothing in the score reflects it.
scenarios.path: Brent $75–90; MOVE 72–82; risk premium $3–12/bbl; score holds 27.

scenarios.name: Mediated pause — the strait reopens
scenarios.desc: Sharply higher, from the 5% low it hit yesterday, on the first negotiating track of this war that both governments confirm. Two US cabinet officials said on 4 Aug a deal could land within days. A signed corridor agreement starts the ten-session maritime clock and would give the oil downgrade its missing leg with the price already $5.45 from the anchor. It remains unsigned, undated and conditional.
scenarios.path: Brent $70–80; MOVE under 75; maritime→3–4 on verified traffic, oil→1, escalation→4; score falls toward 21–23.

scenarios.name: Regional relapse — Gulf energy infrastructure hit
scenarios.desc: Lower. No confirmed strike on Gulf energy infrastructure on 4–5 Aug; Aramco’s chief executive said recent Houthi attacks had no material impact on production capability. The exposure is unchanged rather than removed: Jizan out to about 15 Aug, Abqaiq and Damietta unreported since late July, effective spare capacity ~0.17 mb/d, and a 7 Aug Iraqi militia deadline that remains Tier 3 in origin.
scenarios.path: Brent $150+; emergency policy response; HY spreads above 500 bp; score 29–30.

2026-08-05.scenarioShift: Probability shifts from the 4 Aug edition: mediated pause +6 (5→11), the largest single rise, because a corridor negotiation that both governments confirm replaced one that neither could evidence; full war −7 (40→33) on the cancelled strike package, seven days without a reported strike and Gulf-state pressure on Washington; deal collapse +2 (26→28) and now the largest non-war line, because a real negotiation has real and specific failure conditions; contained-but-violent +1 (16→17) on zero tanker transits and a vessel casualty; regional relapse −2 (13→11) on no confirmed infrastructure strike and Aramco’s statement. Probabilities sum to 100. The balance of this map has tilted toward de-escalation for the first time since 30 July, and it rests entirely on an unsigned agreement.
watchlist: The Treasury quarterly refunding statement, 8:30am ET today — it lands hours after this snapshot. Monday’s estimate put July–September net marketable borrowing at $739bn, $68bn above the 4 May projection of $671bn, with $628bn guided for October–December. The 6 May refunding held coupon sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn and promised no increase ‘for at least the next several quarters.’ Whether that guidance survives a $68bn upgrade is the question, and the 30Y refunding leg auctions in the week of 10 August. Note the positioning: the 30Y closed 5.3 bp lower into the statement and let Stage-4 Threshold B lapse in the process. If the guidance breaks, that lapse reverses quickly.

Whether the Iran–Oman corridor agreement is actually signed — Bessent said ‘today or tomorrow’. This is the single event that could move two channels. A signed instrument starts the maritime downgrade clock (traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions) and supplies the mediated-pause leg the oil downgrade needs, with the price already $5.45 from the $72.48 anchor. What to verify before treating it as real: a signed or published instrument rather than a statement, Omani confirmation, what happens to the US blockade of Iranian ports on which the deal is conditional, and the toll mechanism. An announcement does not move a channel — the 3 August episode is the reference case.

The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, 10:30am ET today — and the SPR line in particular. This is the first weekly since the 29 July print for the week to 24 July: crude 404.5 mb and about 6% below the five-year average, gasoline 211.3 mb and 7% below, distillate about 10% below, refinery utilisation 97.2%, and SPR 307.7 mb after a 3.7 mb draw. Refinery utilisation at 97.2% with distillate 10% below average is the mechanism that keeps the political channel elevated independent of crude, and it is the reason Brent at $77.93 has not brought the pump down.

AUTMUSAG’s next print, against a corroborating series that has turned down. The scored series has three consecutive closes above $4.75 and has been blank for 4 and 5 August. The DOE weekly backfilled at $4.079 for the week to 3 August, down 1.7 cents, and AAA’s own regular-grade average printed $4.089 on 4 August against $4.099 a week earlier. Hysteresis means an easing corroborator does not reverse the upgrade, but a backfill materially below $4.75 would change the read on how durable the break is. Watch diesel alongside it: EIA had on-highway diesel at $5.348 for the week to 3 August.

July payrolls on 7 August and July CPI on 12 August, into a market still pricing a September HIKE. The FOMC held on 29 July at 3.50–3.75% by 9–3 with all three dissents FOR a hike. Third-party FedWatch aggregators disagree materially — 82.4% on a September hike as of 27 July against 59% on 4 August — and no reading direct from CME Group could be sourced for 3–5 August, so the level is reported as unverified. ADP was due 5 August and ISM services on 6 August. Both payrolls and CPI land before the 15–16 September meeting, and 5Y5Y at 2.3180% says the market does not believe the inflation argument has been won.

The Minoan Pioneer follow-up, the 7 August Iraqi deadline, and three series to re-verify. The missing crew member and any attribution of the Khasab strike are the immediate items; UKMTO’s last published advisory is Update 079 of 2 August and nothing dated 4 or 5 August could be sourced. The 7 August Iraqi Islamic Resistance deadline remains Tier 3 in origin with Tier 2 regional pickup and no Tier 1 corroboration — it is watched, not used. On the data side: JGLA has no 5 August print and is never carried forward; AUTMUSAG and SOFR are blank for 4 and 5 August; MOVE and VIX printed for 4 August but not 5 August.

methodology.scale: Shock-score scale. Six transmission channels (maritime denial, oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress, political stress, escalation risk), each 0–5, summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch · 8–14 stress · 15–21 systemic-risk watch · 22–30 crisis. Market channels move only on a confirmed close through a trigger; escalation-risk and maritime denial are event-based. Hysteresis: upgrades fire on a sustained break, downgrades only on a sustained reversal past a wider threshold, deliberately, to avoid whipsawing. This edition tests the rule from the de-escalation side for the first time. Brent fell $10.00 in two sessions and the long end rallied enough to drop Stage-4 Threshold B out of satisfaction, while a negotiation both governments confirm appeared for the first time in the war — and no channel moved, because the oil downgrade needs a pause as well as a price, and the maritime downgrade needs ten sessions of verified traffic rather than a cabinet official’s forecast. The 25–26 June whipsaw and the 3 August announcement that never became an event are the two reference cases, and both point the same way. A one-session repricing is not a regime change.
methodology.scaleCap: Scale cap — binding on five of six channels, and now cutting the other way. Maritime and escalation have been pinned at 5/5 since 10 and 9 July, Treasury since 14 July, US inflation since 31 July and political stress since 4 August. Only oil, at 2/5, retains any upward range — three points in a thirty-point scale. The consequence readers have been asked to hold for a month is that further geopolitical deterioration cannot raise this score. This edition surfaces the mirror image: a genuine de-escalation cannot lower it either, until it has persisted long enough to move an event channel off its maximum. Brent fell $10.00, Threshold B lapsed, and the score did not move a point. A flat 27 should be read as a saturated scale, not as a stable situation — and that now cuts in both directions.

analysis.intro: The shock holds at 27/30 and no channel moved, and this time the composition barely moved either — which is itself the finding. Wednesday was the first session in five that did not reprice something: Brent closed seven cents lower, the curve fell 1.0 to 1.3 bp, and the whole US session ran ten cents ABOVE my morning Brent snapshot after Tuesday’s $3.99 miss. Underneath that calm the two dated tests this monitor had been pointing at for a week both landed and both landed benign. Treasury held coupon sizes at exactly the guided 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn, and the EIA weekly showed crude building 2.5 mb. The long end took the statement as permission: the 30Y closed at its lowest since 28 July and MOVE fell 3.98 to 73.58, its lowest since 20 July and the first close below the 75 leg of the Treasury downgrade since 29 July. On the news side the corridor negotiation gained architecture — agreed coordinates, a 60-day interim mechanism, mine clearing targeted at 30 days — and simultaneously gained a threat: Reuters reported Iran warning three Gulf foreign ministers and Pakistan’s army chief that it would hit Gulf energy infrastructure if Washington struck Iranian infrastructure. The correct reading of a quiet tape is not that the risk fell. It is that the market has now priced the deal and the fiscal test, and has priced neither the seven-day-old strike package Trump says could be sent ‘up again’ nor the retaliation Tehran has just described in detail.

bondYield.title: (i) Treasury — held at 5 (max), and for the first time in the war one leg of its downgrade is satisfied.
bondYield.text: The refunding statement was the event. Treasury held nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes at the levels guided on 6 May — 3Y $58bn, 10Y $42bn, 30Y $25bn inside a $125bn August package — three days after telling the market it would need to borrow $739bn this quarter against the $671bn projected in May. The supply test that armed Stage-4 Threshold A therefore did not fire. What did move is volatility: MOVE closed 73.58, down 3.98 on the session and 9.44 from Friday’s 83.02, its lowest since 20 July, and BELOW the 75 line that forms the second leg of this channel’s downgrade. At 73.58 the index is 0.20 points from its 73.38 pre-war anchor; rates volatility has round-tripped the entire war. The downgrade still fails, and it fails on the other leg: the 30Y closed 5.1680%, 16.80 bp above the 5.00% line. That matters more than it looks. The last time both legs were simultaneously in range was 17 July, when MOVE was 70.88 and the 30Y was 5.0690% — a 6.90 bp gap. Today the volatility leg is satisfied outright and the yield leg is two and a half times further away than it was a month ago. The downgrade has rotated rather than approached, and the honest description of this channel is that it is pinned at 5 by a long end that has repriced war risk without repricing the fiscal arithmetic. Treasury still needs $68bn more this quarter than it said in May; it has simply chosen to fund it in bills and buybacks rather than coupons. One wording change is flagged and reported as unverified at primary level: the statement says Treasury ‘anticipates maintaining’ coupon and FRN sizes, where the prior construction was that it did not anticipate needing to INCREASE them. BMO and Santander strategists, quoted second-hand, read that as a possible step away from forward guidance; the 6 May text could not be retrieved for a word-level comparison.

bondYield.title: (ii) Oil — held at 2, and the session that stopped falling is more informative than the two that fell.
bondYield.text: Brent’s 5 August close of $77.86 is seven cents below Tuesday after a $10.00 two-session collapse, and this morning it prints $78.20, the first up-session in four. The close sits $17.14 below the $95 upgrade trigger and $5.38 above the $72.48 downgrade anchor — the narrowest that gap has been in the war since 10 July, seven cents narrower than yesterday. The downgrade needs both legs: a mediated pause AND a close at or below $72.48. Neither is met, and the reason the price leg has not carried on falling is worth stating. The de-escalation trade ran for two sessions on cabinet-level statements and stopped when the physical facts did not follow: the strait is shut on day 158, UKMTO holds it at SEVERE, TankerMap counted zero transits on 5 August, and the EIA weekly showed distillate stocks falling 3.5 mb to about 12% below the five-year average with refinery utilisation still at 96.5%. Spare capacity was ~0.17 mb/d on the IEA’s July estimate, so September’s 188k b/d is a quota rather than a cargo; Jizan is out to ~15 August; Abqaiq and Damietta unreported since 30 July. The market has repriced the probability of a settlement, not the balance. At 2/5 this channel is the only one that can raise the score, and it is still closer to falling than rising — but the fall requires an instrument nobody has published.

bondYield.title: (iii) Escalation risk — held at 5 (max). The downgrade candidate is stronger in form and weaker in evidence than yesterday.
bondYield.text: Stronger in form: agreed route coordinates, a joint statement in final drafting, a 60-day interim mechanism with a 30-day mine-clearing target, named principals, three named mediators, and a seventh consecutive session with no reported strike on Iran. Weaker in evidence: every element of it is Iranian-sourced or single-outlet. No Omani statement of any kind could be sourced — the mediator has said nothing on the record. Axios and the Irish Times contradict each other on whether the Supreme Leader has approved, and Pezeshkian’s remark that contact with him is ‘very difficult’ makes the approval claim harder to sustain, not easier. Gharibabadi said on the record that there are no negotiations with the United States at all. And the same 24 hours produced Reuters’ report that Iran warned three Gulf foreign ministers and Pakistan’s army chief it would strike Gulf energy facilities, refineries, grids, water and transport if Washington attacked Iranian infrastructure, plus Trump’s statement that the cancelled package could be sent ‘up again’, plus a tanker reporting two explosions off Kumzar this morning. A channel does not come off its maximum in a window that contains an explicit threat to Gulf energy infrastructure and an unexplained detonation beside a ship. The 3 August episode remains the reference case: an announcement is not an event.

bondYield.title: (iv) US inflation impulse — held at 5 (max), and the forward is now 0.67 bp from giving back the break that fired it.
bondYield.text: 5Y5Y forward inflation closed 2.3067% on 5 August — a seventh consecutive close above the 2.30% trigger, a fourth consecutive decline from the 2.3597% war record, and the lowest since 28 July. It has given back 5.30 bp in total. The 10Y breakeven closed 2.2176%, a second consecutive close below the 2.2569% pre-war anchor and also the lowest since 28 July. Spot inflation compensation has now more than round-tripped its war premium; the forward is within two-thirds of a basis point of doing the same. Under the documented rule this channel does not move: the downgrade is 5Y5Y sustained at or below the 2.142% pre-war anchor, which is 16.47 bp away, and hysteresis requires a sustained reversal past a wider threshold than the one that fired the upgrade. The tension between those two statements is real and is flagged rather than resolved: the channel fired 4→5 on a 2.30% break that is about to disappear, while its stated downgrade sits 16 bp lower. What argues for holding is not the rule alone. It is the data underneath. ISM services prices-paid jumped to 70.3 on 5 August against a headline that missed at 54.1, ADP printed +44k against a ~+70k consensus, and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said the same day that ‘if I do not see signs of continued disinflation soon, I am prepared to act’ — having voted with the majority to hold on 29 July. A soft labour print with a hot prices index and a hawkish shift from a median voter is not the configuration in which forward inflation compensation is safely unwinding. Payrolls land on 7 August and CPI on 12 August.

bondYield.title: (v) Political stress — held at 5 (max), but the break has stopped extending.
bondYield.text: AUTMUSAG has backfilled 4 August at $4.75 — one cent below Monday and the first print not ABOVE the trigger since 29 July. The run of closes through the line is three (30 and 31 July and 3 August), not four, and yesterday’s framing that the upgrade was being ‘reinforced’ is therefore corrected: it is intact, not reinforced. The channel does not move. $4.75 is the trigger level itself rather than a retreat from it, the downgrade condition is a sustained retreat toward the $3.52 pre-war anchor, and the series is $1.23 above that anchor. The series is blank for 5 and 6 August and is flagged rather than carried. Every corroborating retail gasoline measure is now flat to easing — AAA’s own regular-grade average $4.0801 on 5 August against $4.0907 a week earlier, the DOE weekly $4.079 with no new release until 10 August. Diesel is the counterweight and it is getting heavier. AAA had on-highway diesel at $5.3622 on 5 August, up 58.5 cents in a month against a flat gasoline, and the EIA weekly showed distillate stocks down 3.5 mb to roughly 12% below the five-year average — the widest deficit of the three product series and wider than the ~10% reported a week ago. Refining, not crude, is the binding constraint on the pump, which is why Brent at $77.86 has not disarmed this channel.

bondYield.title: (vi) Maritime denial — held at 5 (max), and the traffic data moved for the first time in weeks.
bondYield.text: The strait is closed on day 158. Lloyd’s List Intelligence counted 84 total transits in the week to 2 August against 45 the week before, with non-Iranian-linked transits up from 28 to 52 and westbound non-Iranian-linked from 11 to 21 — the largest proportional weekly increase of the war. That is a real signal and it is nowhere near the downgrade condition. Against UKMTO’s own historical baseline of 138 transits a day, 84 in a week is about 9% of normal; the condition is traffic above 25% of normal sustained for ten sessions. UKMTO holds the strait at SEVERE, logs single-digit tanker transits a day, and records 44 vessels redirected under the US blockade as of 3 August; TankerMap counted zero on 5 August; Lloyd’s List notes 65 vessels that entered during the lull and remain trapped, plus 70 more stuck since the conflict began, and two confirmed strikes on ships using the Omani route since 1 August. CENTCOM’s 5 August statement that the southern route ‘remains free and open’ sits awkwardly beside a tanker reporting two explosions off Kumzar this morning, and the monitor reports both rather than choosing. The instrument that would start the ten-session clock — a signed corridor agreement — has coordinates and a draft and no signature.

analysis.stage4Note: Stage 4 is a credit/auction event. Threshold A’s statement leg resolved benignly on 5 August; its auction leg is on 13 August. Threshold B is unsatisfied on a third close.

stage4.title: Threshold A · 13 May 30Y auction, cleared 5.050% — the statement passed, the auction is next.
stage4.text: Treasury’s quarterly refunding statement on 5 August held every nominal coupon size at the level guided on 6 May: 2Y $69bn, 3Y $58bn, 5Y $70bn, 7Y $44bn, 10Y $42bn new issue, 20Y $16bn, 30Y $25bn new issue, 2Y FRN $28bn — a $125bn August package. It did so three days after raising July–September net marketable borrowing to $739bn from the $671bn projected on 4 May, funding the gap with bills, buybacks of up to $38bn off-the-run plus $25bn for cash management, and a possible short-dated CMB around end-August. The specific sequence that would make this threshold live rather than historical was a coupon increase followed by a weak long-end auction. The first leg did not happen. The second is dated: 3Y on 11 August, 10Y on 12 August and the 30Y on 13 August, all settling 17 August. The 5 August close of 5.1680% is 11.80 bp above the May stop, down from 12.43 bp on Tuesday and 22.24 bp at the 31 July war-widest. A tail on 13 August into a long end still 55 bp above its pre-war anchor is what would re-arm this.

stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — NOT SATISFIED, third consecutive close.
stage4.text: The 5 August close of 5.1680% / 4.6127% misses both legs by 3.20 bp and 3.73 bp, and this morning’s 5.1638% / 4.6107% misses by 3.62 bp and 3.93 bp. The satisfied run it ended was 29 July through 3 August, four closes including the 5.2724% and 4.7347% war records of 31 July. Two qualifications stand from yesterday and one is new. The unwind remains a risk-premium unwind rather than a repair of the fiscal arithmetic — Treasury still needs $68bn more this quarter than it said in May, it has just chosen not to raise coupons to get it. The threshold can still re-arm on a single bad auction, and the auction is on 13 August. What is new is that the refunding statement has removed the most obvious catalyst for a re-arm inside the next week, which is why the long end kept rallying after it.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130 — far off, and the index has now round-tripped the war.
stage4.text: MOVE closed 73.58 on 5 August, down 3.98 on the session and 9.44 from Friday’s 83.02, its lowest since 20 July. That is 56.42 points below the threshold and 41.44 below the 115.02 war high of 26 March, so C is not close on any reading. The observation that matters is elsewhere: 73.58 is 0.20 points above the 73.38 pre-war anchor and 1.42 points BELOW the 75 line that forms the second leg of the Treasury downgrade. Rates volatility has fully unwound the conflict while the level of long-end yields has not — the 30Y is still 55.3 bp above its anchor. That combination, low volatility and a high term premium, is the market saying it expects the long end to stay where it is rather than that it has stopped worrying about it. There is no 6 August print and the number is flagged rather than carried as fresh.

analysis.crossAsset: The cross-asset signature is the absence of one. After Friday’s largest upside reconciliation gap and Tuesday’s largest downside gap, Wednesday’s US session moved almost nothing: Brent closed ten cents ABOVE my snapshot, the 30Y 1.26 bp below it, the 10Y 1.01 bp below, the 5Y5Y 1.04 bp below and the 10Y breakeven 1.18 bp below. Two fields are the exception. MOVE printed an actual 73.58 against the 77.56 carried forward, a 3.98-point fall the morning snapshot could not have shown because the index did not print at all on Tuesday; and TTF closed €52.404 against my €55.100 snapshot before bouncing €1.446 this morning, so European gas is still trading the deal in a way crude has stopped doing. Underneath, the routing signature is at its clearest of the war. Henry Hub prints $2.672 this morning, the lowest since 29 April and 12.8% BELOW pre-war, while Asia LNG at ¥3,353 is 100.9% above it and TTF 72.4% above. US natural gas is not participating in this war at all; Asian and European gas are participating entirely. That is a Hormuz-routing shock, not a global-energy shock, and no amount of de-escalation trading has changed it. The dollar fell for a fifth consecutive session to its lowest close since 16 June, which is a US-rates unwind rather than a haven bid, and VIX at 15.81 is 4.05 points below pre-war. The reading to take is that everything except the physical strait has now priced a reopening.

channels.name: Maritime denial
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max). Strait closed to commercial traffic, day 158. Lloyd’s List Intelligence counted 84 transits in the week to 2 Aug against 45 the week before — the largest proportional weekly rise of the war, and still only about 9% of UKMTO’s 138/day historical baseline. UKMTO Update 080 (4 Aug) holds Hormuz at SEVERE, logs single-digit tanker transits a day and 44 vessels redirected; TankerMap counted ZERO on 5 Aug; 65 vessels are trapped inside the Gulf. Coordinates agreed with Oman, joint statement in drafting, nothing signed and no Omani statement of any kind.
channels.downgrade: verified reopening (escorted convoys) with traffic above 25% of normal for 10 sessions → to 3–4. A signed corridor agreement starts that clock; agreed coordinates do not.

channels.name: Oil price shock
channels.rationale: Held at 2 — the only channel that can raise the score. Last confirmed close $77.86 (5 Aug), $17.14 below the $95 trigger and $5.38 above the $72.48 anchor, the narrowest since 10 Jul; intraday $78.20, the first up-session in four after a $10.00 two-session fall. The de-escalation trade stalled when the physical facts did not follow: distillate stocks −3.5 mb to ~12% below the 5-yr average, refinery utilisation 96.5%, spare capacity ~0.17 mb/d, Jizan out to ~15 Aug, Abqaiq and Damietta unreported.
channels.downgrade: mediated pause + close at/below the $72.48 anchor → to 1. The price leg is within reach; the pause leg is NOT met — coordinates are not a pause, and a tanker reported explosions off Kumzar this morning.

channels.name: US inflation impulse
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max). 5Y5Y closed 2.3067% on 5 Aug, a SEVENTH consecutive close above the 2.30% trigger — but by only 0.67 bp, a fourth consecutive decline and the lowest since 28 Jul. BE10 closed 2.2176%, a second consecutive close below the 2.2569% pre-war anchor. Holding is supported by the data underneath: ISM services prices-paid 70.3 on a 54.1 headline miss, ADP +44k against ~+70k, and Governor Cook saying she is ‘prepared to act’ if disinflation does not resume.
channels.downgrade: 5Y5Y sustained at/below the 2.142% pre-war anchor → to 4 (16.47 bp away on the last close, 1.13 bp closer than Tuesday).

channels.name: Treasury stress
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max). The refunding statement held every coupon size — 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn, exactly as guided on 6 May — so the Stage-4 supply test did not fire. The 30Y closed 5.1680%, its lowest since 28 Jul, and MOVE fell 3.98 to 73.58, BELOW the 75 downgrade leg for the first time since 29 Jul and 0.20 pts from its pre-war level. Threshold B unsatisfied on a third close. The 30Y refunding leg auctions 13 Aug.
channels.downgrade: 30Y close under 5.00% with MOVE under 75 sustained → to 4. The MOVE leg is now SATISFIED; the 30Y leg fails by 16.80 bp — wider than the 6.90 bp of 17 Jul when both were last in range.

channels.name: Political stress
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max), but the break has stopped extending. AUTMUSAG has BACKFILLED 4 Aug at $4.75 — one cent lower and the first print NOT above the trigger since 29 Jul, so the run through the line is three closes, not four. Blank 5 and 6 Aug, flagged not carried. All corroborating retail gasoline measures are flat to easing. Diesel is not: AAA on-highway $5.3622, up 58.5c on the month, with distillate stocks ~12% below the 5-yr average.
channels.downgrade: sustained retreat toward the $3.52 pre-war level → to 4 then 3. $1.23 above the anchor; $4.75 is the trigger level itself, not a retreat from it.

channels.name: Escalation risk
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max). The downgrade candidate is stronger in FORM and weaker in EVIDENCE. Form: agreed route coordinates, a joint statement in drafting, a 60-day interim mechanism, 30-day mine-clearing target, seventh session with no reported strike. Evidence: every element Iranian-sourced or single-outlet, no Omani statement at all, Gharibabadi denying any US–Iran negotiation, Axios and the Irish Times contradicting each other on Supreme Leader approval — and Reuters reporting Iran threatened Gulf energy infrastructure if the US strikes.
channels.downgrade: mediated stand-down + talks resume → to 4–3. Requires a signed or published instrument, mediator confirmation, and a sustained window with no vessel casualties.

2026-08-06.scoreTotal: CRISIS band — HELD. No channel moved. Five of six channels are maxed and only oil, at 2/5, can raise this number. Both dated tests landed benign: coupon sizes held and crude built. The composition change worth recording is that one leg of the Treasury downgrade is satisfied for the first time in the war while the other moved further away, and that the diplomatic track gained an architecture and an explicit Iranian threat to Gulf energy infrastructure in the same 24 hours.

whatsChanged.title: 4 · What's changed since the last edition (5 Aug AM → 6 Aug AM)
items: Score holds at 27/30; no channel moved. Treasury holds coupon sizes. MOVE breaks below 75. Iran and Oman agree route coordinates. Iran threatens Gulf energy infrastructure. Source: Bloomberg unless stated.

Treasury held every coupon size, and the Stage-4 supply test did not fire. The quarterly refunding statement of 5 August kept 3Y at $58bn, 10Y at $42bn and 30Y at $25bn inside a $125bn August package, with 2Y $69bn, 5Y $70bn, 7Y $44bn, 20Y $16bn and the 2Y FRN $28bn — exactly the 6 May guidance, and no increase despite Monday’s $68bn upgrade to quarterly borrowing. Buybacks of up to $38bn off-the-run plus $25bn for cash management; TIPS held; a short-dated CMB flagged for around end-August. The 3Y auctions 11 August, the 10Y 12 August and the 30Y 13 August, all settling 17 August. One wording change is noted and NOT relied upon: ‘anticipates maintaining’ replaced a prior construction about not needing to increase, which BMO and Santander strategists read second-hand as a possible step back from forward guidance; the 6 May text could not be retrieved for a word-level comparison. Source: US Treasury press release sb0590.

MOVE fell 3.98 to 73.58 — below the 75 leg of the Treasury downgrade for the first time since 29 July. The index has fallen 9.44 points from Friday’s 83.02 and is now 0.20 points above its 73.38 pre-war anchor, having fully round-tripped the war. This is the first time in the war that one of the two Treasury downgrade legs is satisfied on a confirmed close. The channel does not move because the other leg fails: the 30Y closed 5.1680%, 16.80 bp above the 5.00% line, against a 6.90 bp gap on 17 July when the two were last simultaneously in range. Source: Bloomberg.

Iran said it has agreed route coordinates with Oman, and Axios reported a 60-day interim mechanism. Baghaei said on 5 August that ‘the geographical coordinates of the route proposed by both sides have been agreed upon’ and that a joint statement is in final review and drafting, contingent on no third-party interference. Axios reported the terms as a 60-day interim arrangement — inbound via a northern lane in Iranian waters, outbound via a southern lane in Omani waters, no tolls or fees for 60 days, naval mine clearing targeted at 30 days — with Qatar, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia mediating and Witkoff, Araghchi and Badr al-Busaidi as principals. Nothing is signed. No Omani official statement of any kind could be sourced, and Axios’ claim that Iranian leadership completed its approval on 4 August is contradicted by the Irish Times. Source: Reuters, Bloomberg, Axios, Irish Times, Al Jazeera.

Reuters reported Iran warning three Gulf states it would strike their energy infrastructure if Washington attacks. Araghchi contacted his Saudi, Turkish and Qatari counterparts and Pakistan’s army chief with an ‘unequivocal’ message that Iran would retaliate against Gulf energy facilities, refineries, electricity grids, water infrastructure, transport networks and oil fields if the US struck Iranian infrastructure, invoking the 2019 Aramco attacks. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned Trump urging delay; Riyadh separately warned Tehran it would defend itself. This is the most specific threat to Gulf energy infrastructure recorded by this monitor, and it is conditional on a strike that has not come. Source: Reuters exclusive, 5 August.

The EIA weekly showed crude building and distillate tightening further, with a second SPR draw. For the week to 31 July: crude stocks 407.0 mb, up 2.5 mb and about 6% below the five-year average; gasoline 209.7 mb, down 1.6 mb and 7% below; distillate 107.2 mb, down 3.5 mb and about 12% below — the widest of the three and wider than the ~10% of a week earlier; refinery utilisation 96.5% from 97.2%; and the SPR at 304.8 mb after a 3.0 mb draw, following the prior week’s 3.7 mb. Source: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, 5 August.

A tanker reported two explosions in the strait this morning; the Minoan Pioneer remains unresolved. UKMTO reported, via Al Jazeera at 00:30 GMT on 6 August, a tanker hearing two explosions while transiting about 9 nm south-east of Kumzar, Oman, with vessel and crew safe and no attribution — the third maritime safety event in the waterway in four days. No follow-up on the Minoan Pioneer could be sourced after 4 August: no attribution, no news of the missing third engineer, no salvage report. UKMTO’s latest published advisory is Update 080 of 4 August, which corrects yesterday’s reference to Update 079 of 2 August. Source: UKMTO via Al Jazeera; UKMTO JMIC Advisory Note Update 080.

US labour data softened while services prices accelerated, and a median FOMC voter turned hawkish. ADP private payrolls rose 44,000 in July against a consensus near 70,000, with June revised down to +95k. ISM services printed 54.1 against 54.5 expected, with the employment gauge showing its biggest drop since March — but prices paid jumped to 70.3. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, who voted with the majority to hold on 29 July, said on 5 August that ‘if I do not see signs of continued disinflation soon, I am prepared to act.’ A market-implied September hike probability of about 56% is reported second-hand via Kalshi News and is not verified direct from CME Group. Payrolls land 7 August, CPI 12 August. Source: ADP, ISM, American Banker/CNBC, Kalshi News.

scenarios.name: Return to full war
scenarios.desc: Lower for a second session, and still the modal path. Seven consecutive sessions with no reported US, Israeli or Iranian strike; CENTCOM’s only release since 29 Jul is a change of command; the cancelled strike package has not been revived. But it has not been shelved either: Trump said on 5 Aug the US had been ‘all set for the biggest attack since World War II’ and that ‘we may have to send it up again’, and Vance called Iran’s government ‘fractured’ with factions wanting the war to continue.
scenarios.path: Brent $105–140; MOVE above 90; oil to 3–4; score 28–29 (only oil can rise).

scenarios.name: Deal collapse — talks stall on terms
scenarios.desc: Unchanged, and still the largest non-war line. The architecture became specific and so did the failure conditions. No Omani statement of any kind exists; Gharibabadi denies any US–Iran negotiation; Axios and the Irish Times contradict each other on Supreme Leader approval and Pezeshkian says contact with him is ‘very difficult’; the deal is conditional on lifting a blockade UKMTO records as still being enforced; and Trump has publicly refused the fee mechanism Iran has proposed.
scenarios.path: Brent $88–105; oil back toward 3; Threshold B re-arms; score 28.

scenarios.name: Mediated pause — the strait reopens
scenarios.desc: Higher for a second session, on agreed coordinates, a drafted joint statement, a 60-day interim mechanism with a 30-day mine-clearing target, and a Gulf official telling CNN the odds of a deal by Friday are 50-50. A signed instrument starts the ten-session maritime clock and supplies the mediated-pause leg the oil downgrade needs, with the price already $5.38 from the anchor. It remains unsigned, unconfirmed by the mediator and conditional.
scenarios.path: Brent $70–80; MOVE under 75; maritime→3–4 on verified traffic, oil→1, escalation→4; score falls toward 21–23.

scenarios.name: Contained but violent — blockaded stalemate
scenarios.desc: Lower, mechanically, as the pause line rises — but the content of this path strengthened. The strait is shut on day 158 at UKMTO threat level SEVERE, TankerMap counted zero transits on 5 Aug, a tanker reported explosions off Kumzar this morning, the Houthis say they will now target tankers in the NORTHERN Red Sea, and the score sits at 27 regardless because five of six channels are pinned at 5.
scenarios.path: Brent $75–90; MOVE 72–82; risk premium $3–12/bbl; score holds 27.

scenarios.name: Regional relapse — Gulf energy infrastructure hit
scenarios.desc: Unchanged in probability and materially worse in character. Iran has now explicitly threatened Gulf energy facilities, refineries, grids, water and transport in a message to three Gulf foreign ministers — but conditional on a US strike whose probability fell this session. The unconditional odds are flat; the conditional severity is higher. Exposure unchanged: Jizan out to ~15 Aug, Abqaiq and Damietta unreported since 30 Jul, spare capacity ~0.17 mb/d, and a 7 Aug Iraqi deadline that remains Tier 3.
scenarios.path: Brent $150+; emergency policy response; HY spreads above 500 bp; score 29–30.

2026-08-06.scenarioShift: Probability shifts from the 5 Aug edition: mediated pause +5 (11→16), the largest single rise for a second consecutive session, on agreed coordinates and a drafted joint statement; full war −3 (33→30) on a seventh session without a strike, tempered by Trump’s ‘send it up again’; contained-but-violent −2 (17→15), mechanically, as the pause line rises; deal collapse unchanged at 28% and still the largest non-war line; regional relapse unchanged at 11%, because Iran’s explicit threat to Gulf energy infrastructure raises the severity of that path rather than its probability, being conditional on a US strike that became less likely this session. Probabilities sum to 100. The map has now tilted toward de-escalation for a second session, and it still rests entirely on an instrument no one has published and a mediator who has said nothing.
watchlist: The 30Y refunding leg on Thursday 13 August — the statement passed, the auction is the real test. Treasury held coupon sizes on 5 August, so the supply shock this monitor had flagged for a fortnight did not arrive through the announcement. It can still arrive through demand. The 3Y auctions 11 August at $58bn, the 10Y 12 August at $42bn and the 30Y 13 August at $25bn, all settling 17 August, into a long end 55.3 bp above its pre-war anchor and 11.80 bp above the 13 May stop of 5.050%. A tail on the 30Y leg re-arms Threshold B quickly, and it would do so with MOVE at 73.58 — that is, with the market positioned for the opposite.

Whether an Iran–Oman joint statement is actually published — and whether Oman ever says anything. This remains the single event that could move two channels. What has changed is that the thing to verify is now concrete: a published joint statement with the agreed coordinates, an Omani confirmation from Badr al-Busaidi or the Omani foreign ministry, a US position on lifting the port blockade UKMTO still records as being enforced against 44 vessels, and clarity on fees after Trump publicly refused them. Note what is missing from every account so far: the mediator has not spoken. An announcement does not move a channel; the 3 August episode is the reference case.

July payrolls on 7 August, into a softening labour tape and a hardening inflation tape. ADP printed +44k against a consensus near +70k with June revised down, and ISM services missed at 54.1 with its employment gauge falling the most since March — but ISM prices paid jumped to 70.3. Governor Cook, a majority voter on 29 July, now says she is ‘prepared to act’ if disinflation does not resume. A weak payroll with hot services prices is the configuration that most complicates a September decision, and 5Y5Y at 2.3067% says forward inflation compensation has not yet conceded the point. CPI lands 12 August, before the 15–16 September FOMC.

AUTMUSAG’s next print, now that the break has stopped extending. The scored series backfilled 4 August at $4.75 — back on the trigger rather than through it, and the first print not above the line since 29 July — and is blank for 5 and 6 August. Every corroborating retail gasoline measure is flat to easing. What would change the read is a backfill materially below $4.75; what argues it will not come is diesel, up 58.5 cents on the month at $5.3622 with distillate stocks 3.5 mb lower on the week and about 12% below the five-year average. Refining, not crude, is the binding constraint.

The Kumzar explosions, the unresolved Minoan Pioneer, and the Houthis moving north. A tanker reported two explosions about 9 nm south-east of Kumzar this morning with no attribution — the third maritime safety event in the strait in four days, against CENTCOM’s statement that the southern route ‘remains free and open’. The Minoan Pioneer’s attribution, missing third engineer and salvage status have produced no reporting since 4 August and are carried as unresolved rather than closed. In the Red Sea the Houthis claimed the Wafa off Yanbu and the Daisy in the Gulf of Aden and told Bloomberg they will target tankers in the northern Red Sea, which extends the threat envelope toward Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route.

The 7 August Iraqi deadline, Jizan’s restart, and three series to re-verify. The 7 August Islamic Resistance in Iraq deadline to Baghdad remains Tier 3 in origin (Press TV, 29 July) with Tier 3 corroboration only and no militia activity reported 4–6 August — it is watched, not used. Aramco’s 400k b/d Jizan complex is still targeted to restart about 15 August with no update since 30 July; Abqaiq and Damietta remain unreported. On the data side: JGLA backfilled 5 August at ¥3,353 and has no 6 August print; AUTMUSAG is blank for 5 and 6 August; SOFR backfilled 4 August at 3.66 and is blank for 5 and 6 August; MOVE and VIX printed for 5 August but not 6 August.

methodology.scale: Shock-score scale. Six transmission channels (maritime denial, oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress, political stress, escalation risk), each 0–5, summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch · 8–14 stress · 15–21 systemic-risk watch · 22–30 crisis. Market channels move only on a confirmed close through a trigger; escalation-risk and maritime denial are event-based. Hysteresis: upgrades fire on a sustained break, downgrades only on a sustained reversal past a wider threshold, deliberately, to avoid whipsawing. This edition applies the rule three times in three directions. Treasury holds at 5 although one leg of its downgrade is now satisfied, because the rule requires both. US inflation holds at 5 although the 2.30% break that fired the upgrade is 0.67 bp from disappearing, because the stated downgrade sits 16.47 bp lower at the pre-war anchor — a tension this monitor flags rather than resolves quietly. Escalation holds at 5 although the diplomatic track gained coordinates, a drafted statement and a 60-day mechanism, because a mediator that has never spoken on the record is not confirmation and a threat to Gulf energy infrastructure is not a stand-down. The 25–26 June whipsaw and the 3 August announcement that never became an event remain the reference cases.
methodology.scaleCap: Scale cap — binding on five of six channels, and cutting both ways. Maritime and escalation have been pinned at 5/5 since 10 and 9 July, Treasury since 14 July, US inflation since 31 July and political stress since 4 August. Only oil, at 2/5, retains any upward range — three points in a thirty-point scale. Readers have been asked for a month to hold the consequence that further geopolitical deterioration cannot raise this score; the mirror image now applies with force. This session delivered a benign fiscal test, a fully round-tripped rates volatility index, a third close with Threshold B unsatisfied, and a negotiation with agreed coordinates — and the score did not move a point, because no event channel can come off its maximum until a de-escalation has persisted rather than merely been described. A flat 27 is a saturated scale, not a stable situation.
